title: I/O systems and disk scheduling
relevance: Tests whether candidates understand disk access costs, seek-time scheduling, and CPU–device I/O models that show up in OS interviews and systems OAs.

phases.goal: Establish disk geometry and the three components of disk access time.

must_hit.point: A magnetic disk stacks platters with two surfaces each; surfaces hold concentric tracks divided into sectors (smallest addressable unit), and tracks at the same radius across platters form a cylinder, with a read/write head per surface on a moving arm.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names platters, surfaces, tracks, sectors, cylinders, and heads/arm correctly.

must_hit.point: Disk access time equals seek time plus rotational latency plus transfer time.
Seek time is usually the dominant, most-variable cost and is what disk scheduling optimizes; average rotational latency is half a rotation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Identifies seek as the scheduling target and rotational latency as half a rotation on average.

probes: What are the parts of a hard disk, and what makes up disk access time?

hints.1: Think about how data is laid out physically and what the arm and platter must do before bytes move.
hints.2: Break access into arm movement, waiting for the sector to arrive, then copying the data.
hints.3: Access time = seek + rotational latency + transfer; scheduling reorders requests mainly to cut seek.

phases.goal: Show how common disk schedulers reorder requests and how the CPU learns device readiness via polling, interrupts, or DMA.

must_hit.point: For requests 82,170,43,140,24,16,190 starting at track 50 on a 200-track disk (0–199), FCFS order is 82,170,43,140,24,16,190 with total head movement 642.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls FCFS arrival order and total movement 642 from the worked example.

must_hit.point: SSTF serves nearest first: 43,24,16,82,140,170,190 with total movement 208; SCAN sweeps to an end then reverses (82,140,170,190,→199,43,24,16, total 332); LOOK reverses at the last request (total 314); C-SCAN jumps to 0 after the end (total 391); C-LOOK jumps between extreme requests (total 341).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Can state each algorithm’s rule and the example totals/orders without inventing different numbers.

must_hit.point: Polling busy-waits on the status register; interrupt-driven I/O lets the device interrupt when ready with fixed handler overhead on the order of a microsecond or two; DMA moves a whole block between device and memory without the CPU per word, interrupting once at completion.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts busy-wait, per-event interrupt, and one-interrupt-per-block DMA.

probes: Walk through SSTF vs SCAN on the example queue starting at 50, then contrast polling, interrupts, and DMA.

hints.1: Scheduling reorders pending track requests to cut total head movement; I/O paths differ in how the CPU learns the device is ready.
hints.2: Name FCFS/SSTF/SCAN/LOOK/C-SCAN/C-LOOK rules, then map CPU cost: busy-wait vs interrupt per event vs setup-and-one-interrupt for a block.
hints.3: SSTF nearest-first yields 208; SCAN to end and back yields 332; DMA transfers without CPU per word.

phases.goal: Compare scheduling fairness/uniformity and when polling, interrupts, or DMA is the right I/O model.

must_hit.point: SSTF and SCAN-family cut movement versus FCFS, but SSTF can starve a far request if closer ones keep arriving; SCAN-family avoids starvation by sweeping steadily.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names SSTF starvation risk and SCAN-family’s steady sweep as the fix.

must_hit.point: C-SCAN/C-LOOK give more uniform waiting time by always servicing in one direction, at the cost of the return jump; on SSDs with no heads or rotation, seek vanishes and this scheduling largely loses its point.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions uniform wait vs jump cost, and SSD irrelevance of seek scheduling.

must_hit.point: Polling wastes CPU when idle but is cheap per check; interrupts suit sparse events but have ~µs overhead each; DMA is best for bulk transfers with near-zero per-event CPU cost after setup.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Matches each model to idle cost, per-event cost, and best-fit workload from the comparison.

probes: When would you pick SSTF over SCAN, or interrupts over polling or DMA?

hints.1: Lower total movement is not the only goal—fairness and device type matter too.
hints.2: Contrast starvation under SSTF with SCAN sweeps, then match event rate and transfer size to polling/interrupt/DMA.
hints.3: SSTF can starve; circular variants trade a return jump for uniform waits; sparse→interrupts, bulk→DMA, SSDs make seek scheduling moot.

phases.goal: Apply event-rate reasoning to interrupt livelock, hybrid NAPI-style drivers, and latency-sensitive bounded queues.

must_hit.point: At very high rate (e.g. a 100 Gbps NIC at ~10 million packets/second), interrupts melt down: at 10^7 events/s and ~2 µs each, interrupt servicing alone would need 20 seconds of CPU per second—interrupt livelock; the fix is to switch to polling once packets stream in.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States livelock with the 10^7 × ~2 µs → 20 s/s impossibility and polling as the escape.

must_hit.point: Linux NAPI-style hybrid: take the first interrupt, disable it and poll while the queue stays busy, re-arm the interrupt only when a poll finds the queue empty; interrupt coalescing is a simpler hardware relative (one interrupt per batch).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes interrupt-when-idle, poll-when-busy, and optional coalescing.

must_hit.point: A fixed-capacity ring buffer is O(1) worst-case enqueue/dequeue and rejects when full; a two-stack queue is O(1) amortized dequeue but O(n) worst-case when transferring inbox to outbox—so on a tight deadline path prefer the ring buffer to avoid tail-latency spikes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes amortized O(1) from worst-case O(1) and picks ring buffer for predictable latency.

probes: What is interrupt livelock, how does NAPI avoid it, and why prefer a ring buffer over a two-stack queue on a latency-critical path?

hints.1: Think about what happens when events arrive faster than interrupt handlers can finish.
hints.2: High packet rates force polling; real drivers hybridize interrupt kickoff with busy-path polling; amortized vs worst-case matters for queues.
hints.3: 10^7 × ~2 µs ⇒ 20 s CPU per second = livelock; NAPI polls until empty then re-arms; ring buffer’s O(1) worst case beats two-stack O(n) transfer spikes.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both beat FCFS on total head movement, but SSTF can starve distant requests under continuous nearer arrivals; SCAN/LOOK avoid starvation by sweeping steadily in one direction then reversing.
Circular variants always service in one direction for more uniform waiting time, paying the cost of a return jump to the other end (or between extreme requests for C-LOOK).

Polling: high idle CPU, very low per-event cost, best when events arrive back-to-back. Interrupts: low idle cost, ~µs overhead per event, best for sparse events. DMA: lowest CPU involvement for bulk transfers—CPU sets up once and gets one completion interrupt.
Ring buffer gives O(1) worst-case enqueue/dequeue and rejects when full—no tail-latency spike. Two-stack is O(1) amortized but can O(n) transfer on a single dequeue, which can blow a tight deadline.

gotchas.trap: Assuming SSTF is always best because it has the lowest total movement in the example (208).
gotchas.correction: SSTF can starve far requests if closer ones keep arriving; SCAN-family trades some movement for fairness.

gotchas.trap: Thinking disk scheduling still dominates on SSDs the same way as on HDDs.
gotchas.correction: SSDs have no heads or rotation, so seek time vanishes and this scheduling largely loses its point.

gotchas.trap: Believing interrupts always beat polling for high-rate devices.
gotchas.correction: At ~10 million packets/s with ~2 µs overhead each, interrupts alone need 20 s of CPU per second—interrupt livelock; switch to polling (or NAPI hybrid) when the device stays busy.

gotchas.trap: Equating amortized O(1) with safe worst-case latency.
gotchas.correction: Amortized O(1) is an average over a sequence; the two-stack queue’s empty-outbox transfer is O(n) worst case and can spike tail latency—use a ring buffer on deadline-sensitive paths.
